claims.claim: Identity, also called ego identity, is defined in lifespan development as an individual's complete sense of who they are, including their traits, capabilities, interests, values, and social roles.

The building of identity is a lifelong process, but it takes on critical importance in adolescence because of the number of changes experienced and the sense that decisions could have lifelong consequences.

Erikson's fifth psychosocial stage, identity versus role confusion, typically occurs from ages twelve to eighteen and involves forming a stable and whole identity by first exploring various roles and identities; failing to develop an identity results in role confusion, sometimes called diffusion, which leads to feeling fragmented or lost.

James Marcia built on Erikson by asking two questions that define identity status: Is there evidence of identity exploration? and Is the individual currently committed to an identity? The yes/no answers yield identity achievement, moratorium, foreclosure, or identity diffusion.

In Marcia's framework, identity achievement means the person explored roles and committed to a coherent identity; moratorium means actively exploring without firm commitment; foreclosure means committing without exploratory work; diffusion means low commitment with no active search.
Marcia's identity statuses apply across different aspects of identity, including occupation, sexuality, beliefs, and values.
Self-concept is the mental image or representation we have of ourselves and is the cognitive portion of identity; self-esteem is the motivational and emotional piece.

Research shows that the development of a positive ethnic or racial identity in teens is linked to higher self-esteem, better mental health, and greater resilience against discrimination, and fosters a sense of belonging and empowerment.

Identity continues to evolve over time to adapt to changing roles and contexts; adults periodically reflect on and reformulate their values and goals, and researchers describe moratorium-achievement-moratorium-achievement cycles as new roles and responsibilities appear.

Achieving identity in adolescence represents a pivotal step in identity rather than a permanent, unchangeable status; people keep shifting in occupations, family and friendship roles, and moral beliefs or personal values across the decades.

Psychologist Dan McAdams describes a personal narrative or life story as a level of personality that links personality, priorities, and experiences into a coherent story or identity, and it continues to develop across adulthood.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether identity achievement is a stable endpoint or a revisable position.
positions: Some textbook framings present identity achievement as the successful outcome of adolescent exploration, which can read as a finished state.

OpenStax and Marcia-based research emphasize that achievement in adolescence is a pivotal step rather than a permanent status, with adults cycling through moratorium-achievement as roles and contexts change (e.g., becoming a parent predicts increased identity commitment).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches achievement as a step, not a destination, and keeps the honest note that identity is a journey: statuses describe a person's position at a point in time, and adults re-enter exploration.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Marcia's statuses are primarily about adolescence or about identity generally.
positions: Marcia's original work focused on adolescents' ego identity.
OpenStax applies the same framework to early adulthood and beyond, noting identity consolidation continues in adulthood.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the framework to Marcia, teaches it via adolescent examples, and explicitly extends it to adulthood, matching the source.

sourceRecords.title: 10.1 Theories of Adolescent Socioemotional Development — Lifespan Development (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via Wayback Machine capture 20241108220329 of the canonical openstax.org URL (openstax.org blocks direct fetch). Supports: the working definition of identity/ego identity (complete sense of who they are, including traits, capabilities, interests, values, and social roles); identity building as a lifelong process with critical importance in adolescence; Erikson's fifth stage identity versus role confusion (ages 12-18, exploring roles to form a stable identity, role confusion/diffusion as feeling fragmented or lost); Marcia's two questions (exploration? commitment?) producing achievement, moratorium, foreclosure, diffusion; statuses applying to occupation, sexuality, beliefs, and values; identity achievement in adolescence as a pivotal step, not a permanent status.

sourceRecords.title: 10.2 Emotional and Self-Development in Adolescence — Lifespan Development (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Wayback Machine capture 20241105003052 of the canonical URL. Supports: self-concept as the mental image or representation of ourselves and the cognitive portion of identity, built into a coherent whole that informs overall identity by the end of adolescence; self-esteem as the motivational and emotional piece; the Harter dimensions (scholastic competence, social acceptance, athletic competence, physical appearance, behavioral conduct, self-acceptance). Used only for the self-concept/self-esteem supporting line; facts synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: 10.3 Identity and Culture: Race, Ethnicity, Gender, and Sexuality in Adolescence — Lifespan Development (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Wayback Machine capture 20241108213636 of the canonical URL. Supports: identity development includes ethnoracial identity, gender identity, and sexual orientation; group memberships (e.g., the Hmong student club, soccer teammates) serve an important role in establishing identity; a positive ethnoracial identity fosters a sense of belonging and empowerment; research links positive ethnic/racial identity to higher self-esteem, better mental health, and resilience against discrimination (Rivas-Drake et al. 2014, cited in the chapter). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
